name: ZiiGaat x Vivir Digital Rumba
notes: Fun basshead-leaning tuning, sub-bass emphasis with controlled decay, vocals said to be pushed forward by 2.5-3kHz pinna gain, smooth/safe treble but closed-in on air. Competes at $35 against Truthear Gate (~$20, more neutral-warm, wider stage) and Tangzu Wan'er S.G II (~$20-25, more vocal-forward, better accessories) — both cheaper and actually battle-tested. Kiwi Ears Cadenza II ($49.99) also on the radar but not re-auditioned recently. Revisit with a real listen before trusting these numbers.
summary:
Sound Signature: Neutral / Balanced
Even across all frequencies — versatile and accurate without strong colouration.

✅ Smooth, non-fatiguing treble — sibilance is well-controlled.
🎵 Best for: General listening.

Verdict: Decent (5.7/10) — Gets the job done, some compromises.

name: Hidizs My Lin
notes: Hidizs My Lin — DD+BA hybrid collab IEM. Absolute V-shape tuning: elevated bass shelf (~70 dB, 20–60 Hz) with a significant mid scoop (~10 dB recession at 250–800 Hz), then a sharp treble peak at 6–7 kHz that is the highest point on the entire FR curve. Mids are recessed and instruments lack body. Vocals are thinned out by the lower-mid recession. The 6–7 kHz peak brings perceived detail but causes notable sibilance. Deep trough at 8–9 kHz then steep rolloff limits air extension. Channel matching is near-perfect (L/R almost identical). Build and comfort are above average for the price tier.

name: Tangzu Cai Wenji
notes: Single DD entry-level IEM. Warm-neutral tuning with a strong focus on midrange and vocal presence especially female vocals. Natural, intimate presentation makes it ideal for J-Pop, acoustic, and podcast listening. Bass is soft and non-punchy; poor fit for EDM or hip-hop. Detail retrieval and instrument separation are average. Narrow soundstage creates an intimate but confined presentation. Minimal sibilance and smooth treble make it fatigue-free for long sessions.
